t: Introduction: the beginning of life in bioethics
n: In this lecture we consider the question of the beginning of life from the standpoint of bioethics. In the twentieth century medicine developed rapidly, and its capabilities expanded considerably. For this reason a need arose to reconsider what is a good for the patient, that is, what goodness itself is. This question is linked with the central problem of bioethics, the place of life as the highest value. The problems of this section: the value of life, the time when life begins, the moral status of the embryo, and the ethical and legal aspects of abortion.

t: Life as the highest value: two approaches
n: There are two approaches to life: sacred life and quality of life. Both approaches are conditional to a certain degree. Supporters of sacred life regard life as a sacred, inviolable highest value; in their view, medicine preserves life in every condition, and quality of life is a medical matter. In the quality-of-life view, life must possess certain qualities, and criteria decide whether help is needed. Attention: the life of an organism is not the same as the life of a person, and the quality-of-life view distinguishes them.

t: Sacred life and medical vitalism
n: The sacred-life view is called “medical vitalism” in bioethics. In this view, life is sacred and inviolable. The task of medicine is to preserve life in whatever condition it is; the amount of necessary expense is not taken into account. Life cannot be divided into “especially valuable” and “without value”; quality of life is not a criterion of morality but a medical matter. Supporters are categorically opposed to abortion, euthanasia, examination of the embryo and experiments with the human genome. It is held that life in a vegetative state, too, must be sustained indefinitely.

t: The ethics of quality of life: organism and person
n: Now we consider the ethics of quality of life. In this view, genuine human life must possess certain qualities; it need not be preserved in every condition. To decide whether medical help is needed, clear criteria are necessary. The logic is this: there is the life of an organism, that is, of the body; then it is asked whether it has certain qualities. If yes, this is the life of a person; if no, moral status is lost. Then a decision on help is made on the basis of the criterion. Attention: the life of an organism is not the same as the life of a person; the former is a condition of the latter.

t: Warren's criteria and the relativity of the concepts
n: On Warren's criteria and the relativity of the concepts. In the view of the American bioethicist M.A. Warren, to join the community of persons one needs consciousness, reason, independent activity and communication. In an embryo, a newborn, a mentally ill person and an unconscious patient these qualities are naturally absent for a certain period. Neither concept is absolute, and they cannot be applied separately. Life is recognised as valuable and deserving of respect. Medical resources are limited, so the question of renouncing ineffective and unjustified action is topical.

t: Case analysis 1: a patient in a vegetative state
n: Case analysis: a patient in a vegetative state. The patient is in a vegetative state, with no hope of recovering consciousness. According to sacred life, that is, medical vitalism, even such a life must be artificially sustained by unlimited medical procedures; cost is not taken into account. According to quality of life, life must possess certain qualities, so it need not always be preserved. Question: what decision does each approach give for this patient? Why can they not be regarded as absolute?

t: Quick question 1: distinguishing the approaches
n: Quick questions. First question: to which concept does medical vitalism belong? Answer: to the ethics of sacred life, which regards life as a sacred, inviolable highest value. In vitalism, life in any condition is the highest value; it cannot be divided into “especially valuable” or “worthless”, and cost is not taken into account. Second question: what is the difference between the life of an organism and the life of a person? Supporters of quality of life regard the life of the organism as a condition of a person's life of higher quality. Attention, risk of error! Sacred life is not the same as quality of life. Both concepts are conditional, not absolute, and cannot be applied separately.

t: Quality of life: the WHO definition and factors
n: The WHO definition of quality of life is as follows. According to the World Health Organization, quality of life is an individual's perception of his position within a system of culture and values. It is an integral indicator: it reflects the influence of health factors on how a person perceives his situation. The factors include health or illness, independence, occupation and family. The concept entered medicine from the social sciences; health-related studies began in the 1970s.

t: Assessing quality of life: questionnaires and scales
n: Let us consider the chain of assessing quality of life. Because the patient perceives the situation subjectively, special questionnaires are used. In the final assessment, objective data reflecting the current state of the patient's health are also taken into account. Scales are divided into those with general parameters and those adapted to particular diseases. As a result, subjective perception, through the questionnaire, and objective data become a final assessment, and the scale expresses it quantitatively.

t: The QALY scale: essence and values
n: The essence and values of the QALY scale. QALY stands for quality-adjusted life years; it expresses the quality of a patient's life as a number. The scale was developed on the basis of the concept of utilitarianism. The lower the quality of life, the lower the indicator. Full health equals 1.0 QALY. In chronic disease it is about 0.6 to 0.8, and in a state in which a person cannot look after himself about 0.2 to 0.4. Death equals 0.

t: An example of QALY calculation
n: Let us go through an example of QALY calculation step by step. Step one: quality has fallen because of illness; treatment was started at a QALY of 0.7. Second: the result, the risk of death was eliminated and quality is stable. Third: the patient lived another 7 years. Fourth, the calculation: 7 × 0.7 = 4.9 QALY years. So the treatment extended life by 4.9 QALY years. If life is prolonged but its quality falls, such a life is valued as shorter than a healthy one.

t: QALY, resources and the limits of scales
n: On QALY, resources and the limits of scales. By comparing the cost per one QALY year gained by different treatments, the more economically effective technology is identified. In some countries the assessment of medical technologies by the QALY scale is laid down in legislation. However, no scale is perfect: each person is unique, and there is subjectivity in how a situation is perceived. It is wrong to assess human life, whatever its level, solely by social usefulness or economic efficiency.

t: Case analysis 2: a decision based on QALY
n: Case analysis: a decision based on QALY. In a patient whose quality of life had fallen because of illness, treatment was started when the QALY indicator, that is, quality-adjusted life years, was 0.7. The condition did not worsen, the risk of death was eliminated, and quality of life stabilised. The patient lived another 7 years. Calculation: 7 × 0.7 = 4.9. So the treatment extended life by 4.9 QALY years. Question: can a decision be made by comparing the cost of each additional year? It is wrong to assess life solely by economic effect.

t: Quick question 2: QALY and quality of life
n: Quick questions: QALY and quality of life. First question: what do 1.0 and 0 mean on the QALY scale? The upper limit 1.0 is a fully healthy life, and 0 is the state of death. The lower the quality of life, the lower the indicator: in chronic disease it may be 0.6 to 0.8, and where self-care is impossible 0.2 to 0.4. Second question: what is 7 years × 0.7? Answer: 4.9 QALY years. Attention: quality of life is not the same as social usefulness. It is wrong to assess human life solely from the standpoint of social benefit or economic effect.

t: The beginning of life: the biological viewpoint
n: Let us look at the beginning of life from the biological viewpoint. According to biology and embryology, human life begins with the fusion of gametes and the formation of the zygote. The zygote has an intact nucleus and contains unique genetic material. The sequence is as follows: male and female gametes; their fusion, forming the zygote; cell division. First a group of identical cells forms, then the blastocyst.

t: The pre-embryo and the question of day 14
n: The pre-embryo and the question of day 14. The blastocyst is not yet attached to the inner wall of the uterus. Most of the cells are not yet structured. The blastocyst may divide into two or more parts. For this reason specialists call this stage the pre-embryo. Some specialists hold that until the 14th day of pregnancy various studies can be carried out on the pre-embryo; this is also found in the laws of some countries. Attention: the pre-embryo is not the same as the embryo. From the 14th day the formation inside the uterus is called an embryo.

t: Chronology of embryonic development
n: Let us look at the chronology of embryonic development. The embryonic period lasts 8 to 9 weeks. From day 75 to 76 of pregnancy the fetal period, that is, the period of the foetus, begins. On day 13 to 14 the primitive streak appears, and individual features begin to show. The heartbeat begins on day 18, and the circulatory system is formed by day 21.

t: Foetal sensitivity: when it appears
n: Let us see when foetal sensitivity appears. The first movement of the foetus is recorded at week 6; at this time it begins to respond to touch. At week 10 the nerve fibres of the spinal cord detect the first neurotransmitters, and brainstem activity is recorded. Some researchers believe the foetus begins to feel at weeks 18 to 19; the ability to process sensation has not been established before week 30. The second trimester covers months 3 to 6. Unconsciousness or insensitivity to pain cannot be grounds for refusing to protect personal rights.

t: Case analysis 3: pre-embryo research
n: Case analysis: pre-embryo research. A researcher wants to experiment on a formation at day 12 of pregnancy and justifies it by calling it a “pre-embryo”. In its favour: at this stage the blastocyst is not attached, the cells are not structured, and the formation may divide. Counter-argument: on day 13 to 14 the primitive streak appears, on day 18 the heart beats, and on day 21 the circulation is formed. Question: the embryo, as a “potential human being”, requires a special moral attitude. Does the day-14 limit take this into account?

t: Embryo status: the main question
n: The main question about the status of the embryo is this: is the embryo a part of the woman's body or does it have a special moral status? Different views on when human life begins rest on differences in determining the status of the embryo. The diagram in Figure 6 shows how status changes from fertilisation to birth. First fertilisation, then bioreduct, that is, the view of the embryo as part of the mother's body. Then the status of the embryo changes, egoreduct, that is, a potential person, and finally birth.

t: When the human person begins: five views
n: To the question of when the human person begins, the literature gives five views. It is said that the stage of being regarded as a human being begins from conception, from day 14, from day 30, from week 7 to 8, or from month 7. The first view: a person's distinctiveness begins at conception; the second, from the moment when division into twins is no longer possible, that is, from day 13. The third view: distinctiveness begins much later, 40 or more days after fertilisation. On this question agreement cannot yet be reached; the debate rests on the potential of the embryo, that is, the potential human being.

t: The embryo is a potential human being
n: The embryo is considered a potential human being. It has a distinctive ontological status. As the length of pregnancy increases, the embryo comes ever closer to the status of a genuine human being. At all stages the embryo retains human values and is their bearer; therefore a special moral approach to it is needed. Attention: a “potential human being” is not the same as a “real person”. This is why supporters of “free choice” do not give the embryo the status of a person.

t: Creating and using embryos: ethical conditions
n: Let us consider the ethical conditions for creating and using embryos. If the embryo is given the status of an individual, creating embryos for research contradicts the principle forbidding the “instrumental” use of people. If the embryo does not have such a status, the potential benefit of therapeutic cloning may outweigh other arguments. Denying the status should not reduce the worth of the embryo: a human embryo is not like a laboratory animal. The creation and use of embryos must be strictly regulated, carried out with the full consent of donors and only for humane medical purposes.

t: If status is not recognised: the question of the social subject
n: What happens if status is not recognised? If the moral status of the embryo and foetus and their right to life are not recognised, it remains a part of the woman's body. Then it can be removed without moral contradiction and without consequences, on medical indication or at the woman's wish, like the vermiform appendix. Therefore the unborn living being is regarded not as a part of the woman's body but as a socially recognised subject of moral relations. Determining the moral status of the embryo and foetus is closely tied to the resolution of the question of terminating pregnancy.

t: Religious views: the entry of the soul into the body
n: Religious views are linked with the entry of the soul into the body. The main confessions take a negative view of abortion but permit it in exceptional cases. From the religious standpoint the question is linked with the time at which the soul enters the body. In the table: in the Church of England the entry of the soul is on day 16 of pregnancy, with an exception permitted up to day 16 if conditions are met. In Islam it is month 4, with an exception permitted up to month 4 if conditions are met. In the second trimester, that is, months 4 to 6, a reaction is formed; for this reason some consider abortion permissible in the first trimester.

t: The embryo and abortion in Islamic bioethics
n: The question of the embryo and abortion in Islamic bioethics. Relying on verses of the Qur'an, Muslims consider that one can speak of a human person from the first week of the fourth month, roughly from day 100. Other scholars, perhaps a minority, link the entry of the soul with about day 40. The Hanafi school is the most flexible on abortion: up to the fourth month abortion is possible if there is a threat to the mother's life. The Maliki school forbids abortion after implantation. The general rule: after the entry of the soul abortion is strictly forbidden; in a conflict between the life of the mother and of the embryo, the lesser of two evils is chosen, and priority is given to the mother's life.

t: Embryo status: two approaches
n: There are two approaches to the status of the embryo. The first view: the embryo is a person and has an inherent moral status; this is the view of supporters of preserving life. The second view: before birth the embryo is not real but only a potential person, and therefore does not have the status of a person; this is the view of supporters of “free choice”. Attention: a potential person is not the same as a part of the mother's body. The embryo is a socially recognised subject of moral relations.

t: Case analysis 4: the embryo and the woman's right
n: Case analysis: the embryo and the woman's right. A woman in the first months of pregnancy asks for an abortion. The decision depends on what status the embryo is given. If status is not recognised, the embryo remains a part of the woman's body and can be removed without moral contradiction. If status is recognised, the embryo is regarded as a socially recognised subject of moral relations, and a special moral approach to it is needed. Question: how do the trimesters, that is, the formation of a reaction in the second trimester, and the religious time limits, that is, day 16 and month 4, affect the decision?

t: Quick question 3: embryo status
n: Quick question: the status of the embryo. What is the ontological status of the embryo? Answer: it has a distinctive status, that is, it is a potential human being. As the length of pregnancy increases, the embryo approaches the status of a genuine human being. At all stages it is regarded as a bearer of human values. The times of the entry of the soul: according to the Church of England, day 16 of pregnancy; according to Islam, month 4. Attention: the embryo is not simply a part of the woman's body. It is regarded as a socially recognised subject of moral relations.

t: The history of abortion: from antiquity to the eighteenth century
n: We begin the history of abortion with antiquity. The timeline is as follows: Hippocrates imposed a strict prohibition; Aristotle, however, said abortion was possible for demographic purposes. He said abortion should be performed before sensation and movement have formed. In ancient Rome the foetus was regarded as part of the mother's body. Christianity equated abortion with murder. In the sixteenth century the death penalty was applied. Maksimovich-Ambodik, by contrast, held that in a critical condition it is necessary to remove the foetus in order to save the mother's life.

t: The history of abortion: the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries
n: The history of abortion: the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In 1852 in Paris abortion became possible on medical indication. In 1869 the British Act defined early abortion as a grave crime. In 1880 a ban was introduced in the USA, with permission given only when the woman's life was at risk; this was at the initiative of the American Medical Association. In the twentieth-century debate the feminist movement played the main role: women's rights and questions of sexual morality. Sanger introduced the concept of “birth control”; later it was also used in the sense of eugenic ideas.

t: Types and gestational limits of abortion
n: Let us look at the types and gestational limits of abortion. By gestational age, abortion is divided into early, up to 12 weeks, and late, 12 to 28 weeks; termination of pregnancy after 28 weeks is called preterm birth. In medical abortion, mifepristone blocks the action of progesterone, and misoprostol strengthens uterine contractions and helps expel the products of conception. Mini-abortion is performed with a vacuum device, and surgical abortion by curettage, that is, scraping. For a woman, abortion is a choice between life and death: for this reason the decision is regarded as the most acute ethical and legal problem.

t: A woman's right to decide: three viewpoints
n: On a woman's right to decide on abortion, the literature gives three viewpoints: liberal, moderate and conservative. According to the liberal view, a woman has the right to decide about disposing of her own body, including having an abortion. In the moderate view the embryo gradually acquires human qualities; in each trimester the balance of the interests of embryo and mother is taken into account. In the conservative view, abortion is deliberate killing; the embryo has basic human rights from conception, first of all the right to life.

t: The experience of the former Union and Argentina
n: Let us compare the experience of the former Union and Argentina. In the former Union in 1920 abortion was permitted to prevent criminal abortions; in the early period it was free of charge in hospital. Later, because of war, famine and disease, a ban was introduced; it was repealed in 1955, and abortion was permitted up to 12 weeks. Here there were 100 to 120 abortions per 1000 women aged 15 to 49. In Argentina, permission was at first only for rape and danger to life, and in December 2020 abortion at the woman's wish was permitted up to 14 weeks. There, more than 350 thousand illegal abortions a year were recorded.

t: Abortion: liberal and conservative positions
n: Let us compare the liberal and conservative positions on abortion. In the liberal position the embryo is part of the woman's body, the woman is mistress of her own body, and the embryo is not a person; the argument is the woman's autonomy, and in medical indication the woman's life is preserved. In the conservative position the embryo has the status of a person. The argument: according to the WHO, about 70 thousand women die each year from the complications of abortion. According to the conservative view the foetus feels pain, so abortion is murder; the key question is viability.

t: The intermediate position and Western European models
n: The intermediate position and Western European models. According to the intermediate position, abortion is possible only on medical or social indication. This position does not morally support abortion as a woman's right. In Western Europe there are three approaches. Prohibition: Ireland, Poland, only when life is at risk. A system of indications: Great Britain, on the basis of risk to life, genetics and health. A system of time limits: Austria, France, Norway, Sweden, up to a time limit at the woman's wish.

t: Uzbekistan: gestational limits and indications for abortion
n: The gestational limits and indications for abortion in Uzbekistan are as follows. First the gestational age and indication are determined. Up to 12 weeks, if there is no contraindication, abortion is performed at the woman's wish in an appropriate medical institution. On social indication, pregnancy may be terminated up to 22 weeks. With a medical indication, abortion is possible regardless of gestational age; the list of conditions is given in legislation.

t: Complications of abortion and contraception
n: On the complications of abortion and contraception. To think abortion safe because it is simple, convenient and free of charge is a mistaken notion. Complications of a subsequent pregnancy and delivery, gynaecological diseases, that is, inflammation and tumours, and infertility may be observed. In the course of abortion, complications of anaesthesia, perforation of the uterus, and external and internal bleeding are possible. In 1994 the World Medical Association adopted a statement: the use of contraceptives is the right of all women.

t: Criminal abortion: Articles 114 and 115 of the Criminal Code
n: Criminal abortion is dealt with in Articles 114 and 115 of the Criminal Code. In criminal abortion, the gestational age and the method of termination do not matter. Under Article 114, termination of pregnancy outside an institution or by a person without the right to do so, and also where it is medically impossible, is criminal abortion. Article 115 deems it a crime to coerce a woman into an abortion. If the woman terminates the pregnancy herself or others do so, the woman is not liable. Medical prohibitions: inflammation of the genital organs, a purulent focus, an acute infectious disease, a gestational age over 12 weeks. Termination of pregnancy less than six months after a previous abortion is also forbidden.

t: Case analysis 5: abortion and legal liability
n: Case analysis: abortion and legal liability. A person with no right to do so terminated a pregnancy outside a medical institution. Question: which article of the Criminal Code does this situation fall under? Article 114 of the Criminal Code: termination of pregnancy outside an institution or where medically impossible, and the act of a person without the right to do so, are also criminal. Medical contraindications: inflammation of the genital organs, purulent foci, acute infectious diseases and a gestational age of more than 12 weeks. Attention: in criminal abortion, the gestational age and method do not matter. If the woman terminates the pregnancy herself she is not liable, but coercing a woman is a crime under Article 115.

t: Conclusion: the value of life, embryo status and law
n: Let us conclude. On the value of life there are two approaches: life is sacred, that is, medical vitalism, and quality of life. Neither is absolute; they are applied in balance. In QALY, death equals zero. An example: at a quality of 0.7, another 7 years gives 4.9 QALY years. The scale is imperfect: it is wrong to assess life solely by usefulness. Life begins with the zygote. The embryo, as a potential human being, requires special treatment. On abortion there are liberal, conservative and intermediate positions. In Uzbekistan abortion is possible at the woman's wish up to 12 weeks, on social indication up to 22 weeks, and on medical indication regardless of gestational age.
